summary: TESLA gives source authentication for multicast, with low overhead, tolerance for packet loss, and loose time synchronization between sender and receivers. This document covers how a receiver bootstraps, getting the starting information needed to begin using TESLA. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: When a teacher speaks to a big class, students want proof it is really her. This explains how a new student gets the first clue needed to start checking.

questions: how does tesla multicast authentication start
how does mikey carry tesla parameters
what is the tesla initial key
how does tesla time synchronization work
subtitle: How a receiver gets the starting settings and first key for TESLA multicast authentication, carried inside MIKEY.

tldr.problem: TESLA lets many receivers check who sent a multicast stream, but it only works if every receiver knows the TESLA parameters and the sender's initial key before the session starts. The SRTP mapping for TESLA does not say how to deliver them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how to carry the TESLA policy and the initial key inside MIKEY messages, using a new TESLA policy type in the Security Policy payload and a new TESLA I-Key type in the General Extension payload.
tldr.outcome: The parameters get the authentication and integrity protection of the MIKEY exchange that carries them. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: General Extension type for initial key

today: RFC 4442 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines how TESLA parameters are carried in MIKEY, as a companion to RFC 4383.

sections.title: Why TESLA Needs Bootstrapping
sections.content:
In a group, members normally share one key, so that key cannot prove which member sent a message. TESLA (Timed Efficient Stream Loss-tolerant Authentication, RFC 4082) solves this for multicast with MAC chaining and loose time synchronization between the sender and the receivers.

RFC 4383 describes how TESLA is used with SRTP, but it does not say how its parameters reach the receivers. This document fills that gap by using the Multimedia Internet Keying protocol, MIKEY (RFC 3830), to distribute the TESLA policy and the initial key before the multicast session starts.

The RFC only covers distributing the parameters, not generating them. It requires that authentication and integrity MUST be provided when sending the parameters, especially the initial key, and that confidentiality MAY be provided.
sections.plainLanguage: TESLA is a way for a crowd of listeners to check who is talking. But each listener first needs the starting rules and a first secret clue. This RFC says how to hand those out safely.

sections.title: The TESLA Parameters
sections.content:
The parameters come from RFC 4383, with defaults taken from its Section 6.2. They fall into a few groups:

  • The one-way function F(x) that derives the keys in the chain, and F'(x) that derives the key for the TESLA MAC. The default for both is HMAC-SHA1.
  • The key lengths: 160 bits by default for the chain keys and for the MAC key, and 80 bits for the TESLA MAC output.
  • Timing: the start of the session, the interval duration in milliseconds, and the key disclosure delay counted in intervals.
  • The length of the key chain, which depends on the expected duration of the stream, and the initial key of the chain to which the sender has committed.

One parameter from RFC 4383, the lag of the receiver clock relative to the sender clock, is left out because it can be computed. MIKEY already needs synchronized clocks, and Section 4.3 describes an option to measure clock drift through MIKEY.
sections.plainLanguage: The note holds the rules of the game: which scrambling recipe to use, how long each secret lasts, how long to wait before a secret is revealed, and the first secret clue.

sections.title: The Security Policy Payload and TESLA Policy
sections.content:
MIKEY already has a Security Policy (SP) payload that describes the policy for one security protocol, but it only defined the value 0 (SRTP) for its Prot type field. This RFC adds a second value, 1, for TESLA. The payload carries Next payload, Policy no, Prot type, a 16-bit Policy param length and the Policy param data, which is a series of Type/Length/Value entries with an 8-bit type and an 8-bit length.

For TESLA, the policy types are listed in the table below. The values for the start of the session and the local timestamp of the media receiver SHALL be sent in NTP-UTC format, one of the options in Section 6.6 of RFC 3830. A four-byte integer for the interval duration and a two-byte integer for the key disclosure delay are RECOMMENDED.

The PRF and the TESLA MAC are each identified by a one-byte value. The only value defined is 0, meaning HMAC-SHA1. Policy type 9 is optional; it SHOULD be used only with the in-band time synchronization method and omitted otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY already had a form for describing the rules of one kind of protection. This RFC adds a new box on that form that says 'this rule sheet is for TESLA', plus lines for each TESLA setting.

sections.title: Time Synchronization
sections.content:
TESLA needs to know the clock drift between sender and receivers so that receivers can judge when a disclosed key is still valid. MIKEY also needs synchronized time for replay protection in its one-roundtrip methods. The RFC offers two ways to synchronize.

Out-of-band with NTP (RFC 1305) is the RECOMMENDED approach. It lets the faster half-roundtrip MIKEY variants be used, but it needs an extra protocol.

In-band, sketched in Section 3.3.1 of RFC 4082, may be used when the media receiver is also the MIKEY initiator. The receiver sends its local time t_r in the timestamp payload. The data sender replies with its own time t_s, echoes t_r and includes the TESLA policy payload. The receiver then computes D_t = t_s - t_r + S, where S is an estimated bound on the clock drift during the session.

The in-band method needs no extra protocol, but it requires a full MIKEY handshake and only works in one direction, with the receiver as initiator.
sections.plainLanguage: For the secret clues to work, everyone's clocks need to be nearly in step. You can borrow a shared clock, or the listener can swap times with the speaker once and work out the difference.

sections.title: Carrying the Initial Key
sections.content:
The initial key travels in MIKEY's General Extension payload, which exists so MIKEY can be extended without defining a new payload each time. It can appear in any MIKEY message and sits in the authenticated or signed part of the message.

The payload has a Next payload field, an 8-bit Type, a 16-bit Length giving the size of the data in bytes, and the Data itself. MIKEY already defined type 0 (Vendor ID) and 1 (SDP IDs). This RFC adds type 2, TESLA I-Key, whose data is the TESLA initial key.
sections.plainLanguage: MIKEY has a general-purpose envelope for extra items. This RFC says that envelope type number 2 holds the first secret clue.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC does not provide authentication or integrity itself. It relies on MIKEY for that, so the security considerations of TESLA, of the TESLA SRTP mapping, of SRTP and of MIKEY all apply. It walks through five threats:

  • Man-in-the-middle: parameters exchanged without mutual authentication can be tampered with. The exchange MUST be authenticated and integrity protected, at the same or a higher level of security.
  • Downgrading: an attacker could edit a list of algorithms to force the weakest one, so bootstrapping MUST be integrity protected and authenticated.
  • Denial of service: changing the key disclosure delay or interval duration would make the parties disagree and disrupt the stream later. Integrity protection lets the recipient detect this.
  • Replay: a freshness guarantee MUST be provided, and the key exchange MUST yield a unique, fresh session key bound to the protocol session.
  • Traffic analysis: confidentiality is available only from the MIKEY methods using public key or symmetric key encryption. The initial hash key does not need confidentiality because of the properties of a hash chain.
sections.plainLanguage: If a sneaky person swapped the note, everyone would play by the wrong rules. So the note is sent inside a locked, signed envelope from MIKEY, and each envelope must be fresh so an old one cannot be reused.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added the value 1 (TESLA) to the MIKEY Prot type registry and the value 2 (TESLA I-Key) to the MIKEY General Extension Type registry. It also created two new registries, TESLA-PRF and TESLA-MAC, each holding HMAC-SHA1 with value 0.

Values up to and including 240 are assigned after expert review by the MSEC working group or its designated successor. Values 241 to 255 are reserved for private use.
sections.plainLanguage: A central list keeps track of the numbers. This RFC asks for new entries so that everyone uses the same number for TESLA and for the first secret clue.

viz.caption: TESLA POLICY TYPES IN THE SECURITY POLICY PAYLOAD

items.label: PRF identifier
items.desc: Identifies the function realising F(x) and F'(x). Value 0 is HMAC-SHA1.

items.label: Interval duration
items.desc: In milliseconds; a four-byte integer is RECOMMENDED.

items.label: Local timestamp, media receiver
items.desc: Optional; used with in-band time synchronization, NTP-UTC format.

messages.label: MIKEY initiator message
messages.note: Includes the receiver's local timestamp t_r, which it also stores.

messages.label: MIKEY responder message
messages.note: Includes the sender's time t_s, the TESLA policy payload and the echoed t_r.
